entry.evidence: However, experimental results in Figs. 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 show significant north-south asymmetry, and all the more as S increases.

steps.action: Took from Pedlosky & Greenspan and later sliced-cylinder studies the expectation that a sloping base produces westward-propagating Rossby waves that dominate spin-up, with north-south symmetric wave fields in all known analyses.
steps.quote: The presence of the base slope gives rise to two-dimensional vorticity waves (i.e. Rossby waves)

steps.action: Took from their own earlier theory the prediction that stratified Rossby waves are confined to a layer of height S^-1/2 above the slope, with speed and decay increasing with S.
steps.quote: Munro & Foster [20, 21] extended consideration to spin-up of a linearly stratified fluid in sliced square and circular cylinders

steps.action: Framed the aim as describing the horizontal and vertical structure of the Rossby waves from streamline maps at different heights, to show the S-dependent depth structure.
steps.quote: in order to elucidate the S-related depth-dependence of the motion

steps.action: Set laboratory conditions: a sealed acrylic square tank (L = 35 cm, slope 10°) on a turntable, filled with homogeneous or linearly stratified salt water and spun up from Ω−ΔΩ to Ω.
steps.quote: The experiments were performed in a transparent acrylic tank with a square plan-view section of width

steps.action: Designed the test by fixing ε = 0.02 and E ≤ O(1e-5), varying the Burger number from 0 to 20 across six experiments, and repeating each run with the light sheet at two heights.
steps.quote: it is the Burger number that affects the formation and structure of the stratified Rossby waves, which here was varied between

steps.action: Measured horizontal velocity and vertical vorticity with two-dimensional PIV in the co-rotating frame, then computed the streamfunction by solving the Poisson equation with successive line over-relaxation.
steps.quote: Measurements of fluid velocity were obtained using two-dimensional PIV.

steps.action: Observed for S = 0 a central anticyclone, then alternating cyclonic and anticyclonic waves forming at the east wall and moving west, with corner secondary vortices and merging events, until the fluid is mostly spun up.
steps.quote: alternating cyclonic and anticyclonic vorticity waves, which originate adjacent to the eastern sidewall and propagate westwards across the slope

steps.action: Repeated experiment A at a second height (z = 0.30h) and found no difference, consistent with Taylor-Proudman two-dimensionality for the homogeneous case.
steps.quote: we found no discernible difference between these data and those shown in Fig. 2

steps.action: Observed for S = 0.5 a weak north-south asymmetry (cyclonic wave north of the centreline, anticyclonic wave south), faster wave damping, a residual anticyclone with corner cells, and slight z-dependence in a repeat at z = 0.3h.
steps.quote: there is a weak north-south asymmetry clearly evident in the structure of the vorticity waves

steps.action: Established that the north-south asymmetry recurs at S = 1.1, where waves are also more strongly damped, so the asymmetry persists and grows as S is varied.
steps.quote: The distinct north-south asymmetry in the alternating wave structure is again clearly evident.

steps.action: Compared the two light-sheet heights for S = 1.1, 5 and 10: the first cyclonic wave is confined towards the north wall higher up and is absent at z = 0.35h for S = 5 and 10.
steps.quote: the cyclonic wave structure is confined further northwards in a narrow region close to the northern sidewall, as it moves westwards

steps.action: Compared the observed vertical trapping with the S^-1/2 trapping height predicted in their circular sliced-cylinder analysis and found general agreement.
steps.quote: In general, the data presented here are in agreement with this result

steps.action: Estimated first-wave traverse times of about 40, 30, 15 and 10 for S = 0.5, 1.1, 5 and 10, showing that wave speed increases with S.
steps.quote: the wave speed increases with increasing S

steps.action: Summarized the leading-order quasi-geostrophic theory of their 2014 paper (pressure equation, boundary conditions, eigenvalue problem, Ekman damping rates).
steps.quote: A complete theoretical treatment of the small-Rossby number spin up is contained in Munro & Foster [20]

steps.action: Computed the instantaneous streamlines of a leading-order Rossby mode for S = 0.5 over one period; the pattern propagates westward and is north-south symmetric.
steps.quote: Instantaneous streamlines for a particular time-periodic Rossby mode are shown in Fig. 7

steps.action: Compared the computed mode (Fig. 7) with experiment B (Fig. 3): westward propagation matches, but the theory's north-south symmetry mismatches the observed asymmetry.
steps.quote: the distinct north-south asymmetry evident in the experimental results stands in stark constant with the north-south symmetry in the theoretical results

steps.action: Derived the second-order (O(α)) problem and showed that the (x−1/2) multiplier in its boundary forcing makes p2 north-south asymmetric.
steps.quote: However, working to the next order in the asymptotic series

steps.action: Kept the Rossby-wave framework and revised the auxiliary instead: the one-term truncation is judged unreliable for mode shapes at α = 0.175, and the full second-order solution is deferred.
steps.quote: is sufficiently large to make a one-term solution not particularly reliable in terms of Rossby-wave mode shapes.

steps.action: Kept the claims that westward Rossby waves accomplish spin-up at small S and that, for S much beyond 1, the waves are trapped in a layer scaling with S^-1/2 above the slope.
steps.quote: As S is increased much beyond 1, the Rossby waves become increasingly trapped in a layer above the mean slope elevation

steps.action: Raised boundary-layer eruption, whose time scale matches the Ekman damping time, as a rival origin of the early vortices.
steps.quote: It is noteworthy that the boundary-layer eruption time scale is precisely the same order

steps.action: Excluded boundary-layer eruption for the early vortices of Fig. 3(a–d) by comparing them with the computed Rossby mode of Fig. 7.
steps.quote: it is clear that the vortices in Fig. 3(a–d) are, in fact, in the Rossby-wave structure, and NOT due to boundary-layer eruption

steps.action: Kept the conclusion that the leading-order theory fails because the slope is too large, and that a second-order correction is needed to produce the observed asymmetry.
steps.quote: A second-order correction is required in order to exhibit the north-south asymmetry so much in evidence in the experiments.

Yes; horizontal streamline maps from PIV at two heights
Describe the horizontal and vertical wave structure and its dependence on S; explain the asymmetry
Leading-order symmetric theory vs an O(α) correction; boundary-layer eruption vs Rossby-wave structure for the early vortices

Asymmetry recurs across S values; the homogeneous run repeated at a second height; no quantified uncertainty
Leading-order theory inadequate; asymmetry attributed to the second-order term (best explanation, untested)

end.claim: The observed north-south asymmetry of the Rossby-wave field, which grows with S, is inconsistent with leading-order (symmetric) Rossby-wave theory and is attributable to the asymmetric O(α) second-order term, since α = 10° is too large for a one-term solution.

decisive_move.sentence: Deriving the O(α) problem and showing that its (x−1/2)-weighted boundary forcing breaks north-south symmetry is what turns the observed asymmetry from an unexplained mismatch into a claim attributed to second-order effects.

gates.evidence: Action: the heights and S range were chosen to show the S-dependent depth structure predicted by earlier theory (§1 ¶5; §2.2 ¶4), but the asymmetry was not sought; it emerged from the maps. Claim: vertical trapping faced the S^-1/2 prediction and could have failed (§2.3.2 ¶8); the headline attribution of asymmetry to the O(α) term was not tested, because the second-order solution was not computed (§3 ¶3; §1 ¶5). Registration: nothing is reported as fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Two-dimensional particle image velocimetry (PIV) with a turntable-mounted light sheet and camera
Successive line over-relaxation solution of the Poisson equation for the streamfunction
Asymptotic expansion in powers of the slope α
Double-tank method for producing and measuring a linear density gradient (Economidou & Hunt)

novelty_claims.quote: This paper provides significant additions to what has been reported in our previous paper [20].
Of the significant new results reported in Sect.2.3, we briefly note three here.
what is particularly noteworthy is the observed strong north-south asymmetry of the wave field.

limits: Sub-claims and statuses: vertical trapping in an S^-1/2 layer is regularity_in_range (qualitative agreement, S = 0.5–10, at only two heights per experiment); wave speed increasing with S is regularity_in_range (four rough traverse-time estimates, no uncertainties); the early vortices of Fig. 3(a–d) belonging to the Rossby-wave structure, not boundary-layer eruption, is best_explanation. The second-order theory was not computed, so the attribution of the asymmetry rests on a symmetry argument, not on a quantitative comparison. The asymmetry is described from streamline maps and is not quantified. Each S value appears to be a single run per height, with no reported repeats at the same height. Apart from the S = 0 baseline, no check is reported that apparatus imperfections (tank alignment, particle density band, light-sheet tilt) do not cause the asymmetry. Inference: the data may come from the same experimental campaign as the 2014 paper, but the document does not say. No review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded.

disagreements.target: Typical Rossby-wave theories (Pedlosky & Greenspan 1967) and the symmetric Rossby-wave analyses in the literature [18, 19, 22, 20]
disagreements.support: Measured streamline maps at S > 0 show north-south asymmetry that the leading-order symmetric theory cannot produce; the authors attribute this to truncation at too large a slope, not to wrong physics.
disagreements.quote: We find that the asymmetry is not consistent with typical [...]

disagreements.target: The authors' own leading-order theory of Munro & Foster [20] (2014)
disagreements.support: The Fig. 7 mode is symmetric while the experiments are asymmetric, and the O(α) term breaks the symmetry; they conclude α = 0.175 is too large for the one-term theory, although [20] had reported good agreement for mid-height velocity profiles.
disagreements.quote: does not compare well with our experimental results because the slope is too large to make the theory adequate, as [...] .
